extracted.intended_audience: employers, franchisors/franchisees, State authorities, legal practitioners, and policymakers affected by or commenting on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding the FTC's final rule on non-compete clauses, including coverage, preemption of State law, severability, effective/compliance dates, notice requirements, and exceptions (e.g., senior executives and franchisor/franchisee relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage exclusion: franchisor/franchisee non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not cover franchisor/franchisee non-competes. Non-competes used in the context of franchisor/franchisee relationships remain subject to State common law and Federal and State antitrust laws, including section 5 of the FTC Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission recognizes franchisor/franchisee relationships may present some similar concerns but the evidentiary record primarily relates to employment non-competes. Commenters argued both for and against exclusion; the Commission concluded franchisor/franchisee non-competes will continue to be governed by State common law and antitrust law and are excluded from the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds it has the authority to promulgate regulations that preempt inconsistent State laws under section 6(g), together with section 5, of the FTC Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without an express preemption provision, Federal statutes and regulations preempt conflicting State laws under conflict preemption doctrine. The Commission cites precedent that 'Federal regulations have no less pre-emptive effect than Federal statutes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Express preemption provision (§910.4) and regulatory floor concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes an express preemption provision at §910.4 that preempts State laws to the extent they conflict with the final rule, while not preempting State laws that offer greater protection than the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM framed the rule as establishing a regulatory floor, not a ceiling: when a State law offers greater protection, employers can comply with both. The final rule’s §910.4 was modified to clarify scope and to explain that States may continue to enforce laws that restrict non-competes and do not conflict with the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of State authority and private rights of action (§910.4(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: States may continue to enforce in parallel laws that restrict non-competes and do not conflict with the final rule, and persons retain the right to bring a claim or regulatory action under State laws unless those laws conflict with the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §910.4(b) expressly references State common law, antitrust law, and consumer protection law. The provision is intended to encourage concurrent enforcement, recognize private rights of action under State law, and curb preemption being used as a defense to avoid State restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of preemption—narrower State bans preserved as parallel enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws that restrict non-competes and do not conflict with the final rule are not preempted even if the scope of the State restrictions is narrower than that of the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If a State law bars non-competes only for workers earning less than $150,000 per year, that State may continue to enforce its ban for those workers, while all non-competes covered by the final rule remain unlawful. The rule supersedes State law only to the extent it would permit conduct the final rule forbids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption does not cover State antitrust, consumer protection, or common law unless conflicting
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule will not be construed to annul or exempt any person from complying with State statutes, regulations, orders, interpretations, including State antitrust and consumer protection laws and State common law, except to the extent those laws would permit conduct that is an unfair method of competition under §910.2(a) or conflict with the notice requirement in §910.2(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that many State enforcement avenues remain viable and that State-based penalties and remedies can supplement federal enforcement so long as there is no direct conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability (§910.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any provision of the final rule is held invalid or unenforceable either facially or as applied, such invalidity shall not affect the application of the provision to other persons or circumstances or the validity or application of other provisions; provisions and applications are severable from the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers invalidation, stays, or partial inapplicability, and the Commission intends remaining elements/applications to remain in force. Examples include severability across specific restrictions, categories of workers (e.g., senior executives), notice/enforcement provisions, and other parts of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding: use of non-competes is an unfair method of competition under section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that the use of non-competes is an unlawful unfair method of competition under section 5 of the FTC Act because such restraints are restrictive and exclusionary and tend to negatively affect competitive conditions in labor markets and product and service markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For workers who are not senior executives, the Commission further finds non-competes are exploitative and coercive. These findings are supported principally by empirical evidence on changes in enforceability and quantified in the regulatory impact analysis (Part X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and compliance period: 120 days after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adopts a uniform effective date and compliance period of 120 days after publication in the Federal Register; compliance with the final rule is required on that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission reduced the compliance period from the NPRM's proposed 180 days to 120 days to bring relief sooner, while balancing burdens on covered entities. A 120-day effective date also complies with the Congressional Review Act timing for a 'major rule'.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rescission requirement; prohibition on enforcement for most workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final rule, employers will not need to rescind existing non-competes; rather, employers are prohibited from enforcing non-competes they entered into prior to the effective date with workers other than senior executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission removed the rescission requirement proposed in the NPRM to simplify compliance. Employers must, however, provide notice (see §910.2(b)(1)) to workers with existing non-competes who are not senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement for existing non-competes (§910.2(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are required to provide notice to workers with existing non-competes who are not senior executives. The final rule provides model safe harbor language satisfying the notice requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may provide notice on paper, by mail, by email, or by text. Employers are exempt from the notice requirement where the employer has no record of a street address, email address, or mobile telephone number for the worker. The Commission simplified the notice requirement to allow mass communications (e.g., mass email).

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for employers to protect confidential business information
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent employers have confidential business information, trade secrets, or other investments to protect, they may assess lawful options to protect that information after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes many workers subject to non-competes are already subject to NDAs (95.6% cited) and in many cases new protections will be unnecessary. Employers and workers may agree to amend agreements in rare cases where compensation is tied to non-competes that are not with senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion/exception for senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule allows enforcement of existing non-competes for senior executives; the rule distinguishes between senior executives and workers who are not senior executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission determined senior executives are excluded from the ban because their compensation arrangements may be complex; this exclusion reduces the compliance burden and removes the need for lengthy compliance periods for complex contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandfathering for pending causes of action (§910.3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: §910.3(b) provides that the final rule does not apply where a cause of action related to a non-compete arose prior to the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the need to extend the compliance period to allow courts to adjudicate pending non-compete litigation; a challenger can still seek a preliminary injunction against the rule itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical basis and expected magnitude vs direction of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission relies principally on empirical evidence regarding the effects of changes in non-compete enforceability to find that non-competes tend to negatively affect competitive conditions in labor and product/service markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses (Part X.F.6) include sensitivity analyses showing smaller changes in enforceability change the magnitude but not the directional nature of labor market and product/service market effects; this underpins the Commission’s judgment on scope and severability.

rubrics_metrics.name: State enforcement and penalties as supplemental deterrent
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws and State enforcement (including private rights of action under State non-compete laws) can provide additional enforcement avenues and penalties that may be substantial and important as a deterrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission recognizes State enforcement can supplement Federal efforts; the final rule was modified to encourage concurrent enforcement and to avoid preemption of State laws that do not conflict with the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and rejection of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considered alternatives to a categorical federal ban, including a rebuttable presumption of unlawfulness, different standards for categories of workers, disclosure or reporting rules, and relying solely on State laws, but decided not to adopt those alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments on alternatives were solicited and considered; the Commission discusses reasons for rejecting alternatives in Part IX, concluding a clear national standard (with the modifications described) best mitigates the harms of the patchwork of State laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Share the field' partnership with States
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission intends to 'share the field' with States and partner with them in enforcement against abusive non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects an intent to supplement, not wholly supplant, State enforcement resources, acknowledging some residual variation among States while establishing a national floor.
